questions.q: What mistake does this case study identify as the one a team new to multi-system integration projects often makes?
options: Using too many different vendors for a single integration
Choosing one integration architecture and applying it uniformly across every data flow in the project, regardless of each flow's actual, differing requirements
Failing to document any of the integration decisions
Refusing to use any AppExchange connectors under any circumstances
questions.explain: The case study is specifically designed to expose this instinct -- picking one pattern (like 'real-time, event-driven everything') and applying it to every flow, even when different flows have genuinely different freshness and build-vs-buy needs.

questions.q: Why does Flow 1 (inventory levels from ERP into Salesforce) resolve toward a real-time pattern?
options: Because real-time integration is always the more sophisticated choice
Because the ERP system does not support batch processing at all

Because a sales rep promising a delivery date needs current stock, and a stale inventory number is worse than a slightly slower real-time check -- the business cost of stale data here is real and immediate
Because Salesforce requires all ERP integrations to be real-time by default
questions.explain: This flow genuinely needs the freshness that justifies real-time's added complexity and monitoring cost, per Lesson 7's criteria -- the business cost of a stale promise is real, which is exactly what tips this decision toward real-time.

questions.q: Why does Flow 2 (nightly order history sync) resolve toward batch rather than real-time?
options: Because the ERP's reporting warehouse cannot accept real-time events
Because Bulk API 2.0 is the only API Salesforce offers for ERP integrations
Because batch processing is always cheaper regardless of use case

Because financial reconciliation runs on a daily or weekly cadence, so a real-time event stream would pay all the complexity and monitoring cost of Flow 1's pattern for a process that gets zero benefit from the extra freshness
questions.explain: Flow 2 is a textbook batch case specifically because 'a few hours old' costs nothing real for a daily/weekly financial reconciliation process -- paying real-time's complexity cost here would buy no actual benefit.

questions.q: What specific gap does this lesson say to check for before fully committing to the marketing platform vendor's managed-package connector for Flow 3?
options: Whether consent-status mapping -- a likely compliance-sensitive field -- is covered by a genuine, documented extension point, or would require logic the package's hidden source doesn't expose
Whether the connector supports the Spanish language
Whether the vendor offers a discount for annual contracts
Whether the connector was released within the last six months
questions.explain: This directly applies Lesson 13's managed-package extension-point analysis to the compliance-sensitive consent field specifically -- if that mapping isn't a supported extension point, it may need custom Apex alongside the package rather than disqualifying the whole buy decision.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what is the actual architecture skill being tested by this case study?
options: Memorizing a single correct integration pattern to apply to all future projects
Correctly classifying each distinct data flow in a project against its own real requirements, even when the whole initiative sounds like it should have one unified answer
Minimizing the total number of systems involved in any integration project
Always preferring custom-built integrations over any vendor connector
questions.explain: The lesson's closing point is that the real skill is recognizing each flow's distinct requirements and choosing accordingly, rather than reaching for one unified architecture for the whole initiative.
